newsitem.title: USA: U.S. embargo against Cuba turns 35; no end in sight.
newsitem.headline: U.S. embargo against Cuba turns 35; no end in sight.

text.p: The United States' embargo against Cuba turned 35 on Monday, as controversial as ever and unlikely to end soon, supporters and detractors agree.
Eight U.S. presidents have kept the sanctions in place in a bid to punish and weaken Cuban President Fidel Castro, who has dodged assassination attempts and invasions fostered by Washington.
And now the embargo, first approved by President John F. Kennedy on Feb. 3, 1962, has become part of a law that cannot be lifted by executive order.
President Bill Clinton signed that authority away last year when he enacted the so-called Helms-Burton law, which codified all the sanctions imposed on Cuba by his predecessors.
"If there ever was a possibility of Clinton lifting the embargo during his second term, it disappeared with Helms-Burton," Representative Lincoln Diaz-Balart, a Florida Republican told Reuters.
Diaz-Balart, who was born in Havana and is Castro's nephew by marriage, penned the amendment that codified the embargo.
"That is the most important thing I have done in my life," he said in a telephone interview from Miami, home to a large Cuban exile community fiercely opposed to Castro.
The law conditions the lifting of the embargo on a series of requirements, among them a call for free and open elections on the island that Castro has ruled since 1959.

But both Diaz-Balart and the Cuban American National Foundation (CANF) rejected the notion that the sanctions have failed, and argued they only started to bite in 1992, after the demise of the Soviet Union, which long subsidised Cuba.
"By denying Castro an economic lifeline ... he is forced to confront the reality of Cuba's crisis," said CANF's executive director in Washington, Jose Cardenas.
CANF, which lobbied hard and successfully since 1981 for tougher policies against Cuba, believes the embargo pushes Castro to make reforms that undermine his regime's power.

As the island's economy tumbled between 1991 and 1994, the veteran communist leader opened key sectors like tourism and telecommunications to foreign investors. But Castro has been hesitant to allow a domestic private sector to grow.
"The burden of change is squarely on Castro's shoulders," Cardenas said.
Although no friend of CANF's, former U.S. diplomat Wayne Smith, an outspoken critic of Washington's policy toward Cuba, agreed that chances of ending the embargo are scant.
"With Congress in control of the Republicans ... it won't be repealed," he said.
Smith said it was a sad anniversary.

"Ten years from now Cuba will look much different, more like a social democracy, but the United States will have had nothing to do with that transformation," he said. "And perhaps that will be a good thing."
In Cuba, a government newspaper dated the sanctions to the days when Castro started to nationalise U.S. properties after toppling strongman Fulgencio Batista in 1959.
Those confiscations, worth more than $6 billion according to U.S. estimates, laid the groundwork for the economic sanctions and, decades later, for the Helms-Burton law.

That law -- enacted after Cuba shot down two small U.S. civilian aircraft and killed four Cuban-Americans -- toughened the embargo by threatening foreign investors dealing with those disputed properties.
However, John Kavulich, executive director of the U.S.-Cuba Business and Trade Council, said one group has not yet used its political clout in this debate -- American business.
"The U.S. business community is eagerly looking forward to returning to Cuba's market at the earliest possible date," he said in an interview from his offices in New York.
